name: Polypodium leucotomos
lead: Polypodium leucotomos is the older botanical name for Phlebodium aureum, an epiphytic fern native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. Extract from its leaves is sold as an oral supplement, including under the Heliocare name, and has been studied in dermatology as an 'internal' or systemic photoprotective agent [1][4][20].

Decoctions were used in Central American folk medicine, and modern research has examined the extract for conditions including melasma, vitiligo, psoriasis, polymorphous light eruption, atopic dermatitis, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, photoaging and skin cancer [1]. A 2025 systematic review of oral photoprotective supplements found the greatest evidence among polyphenols, carotenoids and Polypodium leucotomos [2].

Reviews also note limits: few trials support supplements as monotherapy or as an alternative to sunscreen, and trials are small with varied formulations [3][2]. In looksmaxxing forums it appears as a supplement to combine with tanning peptides and to reduce the sun exposure needed for a tan [20].

paras: The extract is taken as an adjunct to reduce sunburn, photoaging and pigmentation, sometimes alongside sunscreen [1][2]. A 2009 T Nation poster asked about combining melanotan II with Heliocare and tyrosine to maximise a tan with less time in tanning salons [20].
The extract has been investigated in melasma [10][11][15][16], vitiligo phototherapy [7], actinic keratoses [8] and atopic dermatitis [9]. It has no approved drug indication.

Photoprotection: Wikipedia summarises that clinical studies show oral extract provides photoprotection against UVB and UVA, and that a review of 19 human and 6 basic studies found it well tolerated [1]. A 2019 systematic review and a 2007 nutraceutical review examined its efficacy and safety [12][14]. A 2025 review of 47 studies of oral supplements found the greatest photoprotection evidence for polyphenols, carotenoids and Polypodium leucotomos [2]. A 2021 review concluded that few trials support these supplements as monotherapy, impeding recommendation as an alternative to sunscreen [3].

Recent randomized trials include a 50-volunteer intraindividual study comparing oral nicotinamide with Heliocare Advanced on UVA-induced erythema and thymidine dimers [4], a UVB counterpart [5], and an eight-week trial of a red orange plus Polypodium leucotomos supplement on UVB-induced skin responses [6]. Registered studies examine visible-light effects, minimal erythema dose and skin cancer precursors [17][18][19].

Dermatologic conditions: a randomized placebo-controlled study enrolled 44 patients with generalized vitiligo to test whether oral extract improves NB-UVB repigmentation [7]. A randomized trial examined oral extract, colchicine cream and ingenol mebutate in actinic keratoses [8], and a multicenter trial examined it in atopic dermatitis [9]. Melasma has been studied in registered small trials of 21 and 40 patients [15][16], and a 2025 review covers its dermatologic uses [13].

A review of 19 human and 6 basic studies reported that oral extract was well tolerated with a favourable side effect profile [1]. Evidence is based on small trials with different formulations, so supplements that do not specify the studied extract may not be equivalent [2][12].

The extract is rich in phenolic compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; studies describe reduced UV-induced DNA damage markers such as thymidine dimers [14][4][5]. It does not act as a UV filter.
The sampled community material is sparse. A 2009 T Nation post asks about combining Heliocare with melanotan II and tyrosine [20].
